stem: What is the guiding principle behind the compute decision tree in this lesson?
options: Pick the platform the team already knows, because familiarity beats fit
Start at the most managed option that can run the workload and move down the ladder only when a named requirement forces it
Start with containers, because an image can be moved to any of the other services later
Choose whichever option has the lowest list price for the expected traffic
explanation: Every step down the ladder adds something you must run, watch and pay for whether or not anyone is using it, so the burden should be forced on you by a requirement rather than chosen. Starting with containers is the tempting answer because images are portable, but it adds a registry, a build and image hygiene to workloads that a platform would have run from source.

scenario: A proposal for a new internal reporting front end says "we will containerise it so we have options later". The app is a compiled React bundle with no server code.
stem: Which question in the decision tree settles this, and what is the answer?
options: Question 3, the runtime dependency question: it needs a container because the build tooling is unusual
Question 4, the long-running web app question: App Service, because every web thing needs a web server
Question 1, the static files question: Static Web Apps, because the build output is files and needs no server process
Question 5, the cluster question: Container Apps, because it is the default for containerised services
explanation: The first question asks whether the workload is static files with no server logic, and a React build is exactly that, so it lands on a CDN and never reaches the container question. Choosing App Service would pay for a process that does nothing, and "options later" is a preference rather than the named requirement the tree demands.

scenario: A Functions app on a Consumption plan started as an occasional webhook. It now runs tens of millions of times a month at a steady rate, and the bill has passed what a Premium v3 App Service plan would cost.
options: The workload has crossed from bursty to steady state, so a fixed plan is now the cheaper billing shape
The functions must be badly written, because Consumption is always cheaper than a plan
The app should move to AKS, because a cluster spreads the cost across more services
Nothing: per-execution billing always tracks usage, so the price is by definition correct
explanation: Per-execution billing is near-free when idle and expensive at steady high volume, while a fixed plan is the reverse, so a workload whose shape has changed should change its pricing model too. Consumption being "always cheaper" is the half-read version of the lesson; the crossover is precisely the point where it stops being true.

scenario: A contractor proposes AKS for a five-person team running three small APIs, on the grounds that Kubernetes keeps them portable.
stem: What is the strongest objection to raise in the review?
options: Kubernetes cannot run .NET or Node workloads well, so the services would need rewriting
AKS has no autoscaling, so the team would have to size the cluster for peak by hand
Question 5 has two conditions - a genuine need for cluster-level control and a named owner - and neither has been shown, so Container Apps does the job for a fraction of the running cost
Portability is not achievable on Azure, so the stated benefit is impossible
explanation: The cluster question requires both a real requirement and a person to own upgrades and on-call; without the second the cluster becomes one person's hobby and then their leaving present. Portability is achievable, but it is a monthly cost - nodes bill whether or not pods use them - and paying it to insure against a migration nobody has funded is the weak part of the argument, not the technology.

stem: Which requirement genuinely forces a virtual machine rather than a managed platform?
options: The application needs to run continuously rather than scale to zero
The vendor ships the product only as a Windows installer with a licence bound to the machine
The team wants shell access so they can read log files quickly
The service must connect to a database over a private network
explanation: Installer-only software, machine-bound licences, GPU drivers and kernel-level agents are the cases no PaaS will accept, and they short-circuit the rest of the tree. Continuous running is what an App Service plan does, private networking is available through VNet integration, and wanting shell access is a preference that costs you an operating system to patch forever.

stem: How should a compute decision treat the risk of vendor lock-in?
options: As a rule: always choose the most portable option available so migration is never blocked
As irrelevant, since application code is portable and everything else can be rewritten quickly
As a price to compare: portability has a monthly running cost, so buy it when a funded requirement exists
As a reason to run everything on virtual machines, since an image can be copied anywhere
explanation: Portability is real but it is bought, most obviously in cluster nodes that bill continuously, so it belongs in the cost comparison rather than in a blanket rule. A VM looks portable but you carry the operating system, its patching and its monitoring with you, which is the most expensive kind of portability there is.

stem: Which of these is a trigger that should reopen a compute decision, rather than something to absorb?
options: A new engineer joins who is more comfortable with a different platform
The monthly bill crosses the threshold you wrote down as the crossover to a fixed plan
A release takes longer than usual because the build pipeline was slow
Traffic doubles for one week during a marketing campaign and then returns to normal
explanation: Good triggers are ones you can name in advance and measure: a cost threshold, a platform limit, a dependency the platform will not run, a team change or a funded portability requirement. A single campaign spike is exactly what elastic compute is for, and personal preference is the kind of argument the decision framework exists to settle.

scenario: Three proposals land in the same week: Functions for notifications, AKS for everything and "just a VM" for a new internal tool.
stem: Which question does the most to make all three proposals justify themselves?
options: "Which question in the tree moved you here, and what does it cost at zero traffic and at ten times today's?"
"Has this service been used successfully by another team in the company?"
"Can we deploy it from our existing GitHub Actions workflow without changes?"
"Which option has the highest SLA on paper?"
explanation: It forces the proposer to name the requirement that moved them down the ladder and to price both ends of the traffic range, which is what separates a requirement from a preference. Deployment tooling and other teams' experience are useful context, but they justify familiarity rather than fit, and the highest SLA on paper usually just points at the most expensive option.
